related_questions.question: How many years of work is 40 credits for Social Security?

text_blocks.snippet: To qualify for Social Security retirement benefits, individuals need 40 credits, which typically equates to 10 years of work. This applies to those born in 1929 or later. The credits don't have to be earned consecutively.

list.title: Credits are earned through work:
list.snippet: Social Security credits are earned by paying Social Security taxes on your earnings.

list.title: Earning credits:
list.snippet: You can earn a maximum of 4 credits per year.

list.title: Example:
list.snippet: In 2025, you earn one Social Security credit for every $1,810 in covered earnings. To earn the maximum of 4 credits for the year, you need to earn $7,240.

list.title: Benefits calculation:
list.snippet: The amount of your retirement benefit is based on your highest 35 years of earnings, not just the 10 years required for eligibility.

list.title: Other Social Security benefits:
list.snippet: The credit requirements may vary for other types of Social Security benefits, such as disability benefits.

list.title: No work requirement for SSI:
list.snippet: Supplemental Security Income (SSI) is a separate program with no work requirement, but it has income and asset limits.

related_questions.question: How to check Social Security credit score?

text_blocks.snippet: To check your Social Security credits, you'll need to access your Social Security Statement. You can do this by creating a my Social Security account on the Social Security Administration's website. This online account allows you to view your earnings history and the number of credits you've earned. If you don't have a my Social Security account and are 60 or older, you'll receive a paper statement three months before your birthday, or you can request one online.
snippet_highlighted_words: creating a my Social Security account on the Social Security Administration's website

text_blocks.snippet: Here's how to check your Social Security credits:

list.title: 1. Create a my Social Security account:
list.snippet: Go to the Social Security Administration's website and create an account.

list.title: 2. Access your Social Security Statement:
list.snippet: Once logged in, you can view your Social Security Statement, which details your earnings history and the number of work credits you've earned.

list.title: 3. Review your statement:
list.snippet: The statement will show how many credits you've accumulated, which are based on your earnings.

list.title: 4. Alternative for those 60 and older:
list.snippet: If you're 60 or older and don't have a my Social Security account, you'll receive a paper statement three months before your birthday.

list.title: 5. Request a paper statement:
list.snippet: You can also request a paper statement by completing and mailing Form SSA-7004.

related_questions.question: How do you qualify for Social Security credits?

text_blocks.snippet: To be eligible for Social Security benefits, individuals generally need to earn 40 credits. These credits are earned by working and paying Social Security taxes. In 2025, you earn one credit for every $1,810 in earnings, up to a maximum of four credits per year. The amount of earnings needed for a credit increases slightly each year as average wages increase.

list.title: Earning Credits:
list.snippet: You earn Social Security credits by working and paying Social Security taxes.

list.title: How Many Credits?
list.snippet: You need 40 credits, which is equivalent to 10 years of work, to be fully insured and eligible for most Social Security benefits.

list.title: Credit Limits:
list.snippet: You can earn a maximum of four credits per year.

list.title: 2025 Earnings:
list.snippet: In 2025, you earn one credit for each $1,810 in earnings, according to the Social Security Administration (.gov).

list.title: Earnings Increase:
list.snippet: The amount of earnings needed for one credit increases annually, according to the Social Security Administration (.gov).

list.title: Staying Insured:
list.snippet: Once you've earned enough credits, they stay on your record, even if you change jobs or have periods with no earnings, according to the Social Security Administration (.gov).

list.title: Full Retirement Age:
list.snippet: Full retirement age for Social Security benefits is gradually increasing to age 67 for those born in 1960 or later.

list.title: Checking Credits:
list.snippet: You can check your Social Security statement online through your My Social Security account to see how many credits you've earned, says Experian.

list.title: Disability Benefits:
list.snippet: The number of credits needed for disability benefits depends on your age, but generally, you need 40 credits with 20 earned in the last 10 years, according to the Social Security Administration (.gov).

text_blocks.snippet: There isn't a direct correlation between Social Security benefits and a traditional credit score. Social Security benefits are determined by your earnings and work history, while credit scores are based on factors like payment history, amounts owed, and credit history. Social Security credits, which are earned by working and paying Social Security taxes, determine your eligibility for Social Security benefits, but they don't affect your credit score.

list.title: Purpose:
list.snippet: Credits determine your eligibility for retirement, disability, and Medicare benefits.

list.title: What it is:
list.snippet: A credit score is a numerical representation of your creditworthiness, based on your credit history.

list.title: Factors influencing it:
list.snippet: Payment history, amounts owed, length of credit history, and new credit applications all impact your credit score.

list.title: Social Security's role:
list.snippet: Your Social Security benefits do not directly impact your credit score.

list.title: Checking your score:
list.snippet: You can get your credit score from the major credit bureaus (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion) or through various online platforms.
